en: Udāna 6.2 Sattajaṭilasutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, the Blessed One was sitting outside the gateway.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Now at that time, seven matted-hair ascetics, seven Jain monks, seven naked ascetics,
seven one-robed ascetics, and seven wanderers— each with the hair of their armpits and body grown long— carrying various kinds of begging bowls,
were passing by not far from the Blessed One.
King Pasenadi of Kosala saw those seven matted-hair ascetics, seven Jain monks, seven naked ascetics,
seven single-robed ascetics, and seven wanderers, with their armpits, nails, and body hair grown long,
carrying various kinds of begging bowls as they passed by not far from the Blessed One.
Having seen them, he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and extending his joined palms toward those seven matted-hair ascetics, seven Jain ascetics, seven naked ascetics,
seven single-robed ascetics, and seven wanderers, he announced his name three times:
“I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir;
I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir;
I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir.”
Then, not long after those seven matted-hair ascetics,
seven Nigaṇṭhas, seven naked ascetics, seven one-robed ascetics, and seven wanderers had departed,
King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, those who in the world are either arahants or have entered the path to arahantship—these are some among them.
"It is difficult for you to know this, great king, being a householder enjoying sensual pleasures, living in a bed crowded with children."
"By enjoying Kāsī sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and ointments, and accepting gold and silver—one cannot know:
'These are Arahants, or these have entered the path to Arahantship.

Rather, Great King, virtue is to be known through association; and that must be over a long period, not a short one; by one who is attentive, not inattentive; and by one who is wise, not by one of dull wisdom."

"By means of social interaction, Great King, purity is to be known; and that, moreover, over a long period of time and not briefly, by one who is attentive and not inattentive, by one who is wise and not dull-witted.

By means of misfortunes, Great King, fortitude is to be known; and that, moreover, over a long period of time and not briefly, by one who is attentive and not inattentive, by one who is wise and not dull-witted."

“Great King, wisdom is to be known through discussion. And that, moreover, over a long period of time and not briefly; by one who attends to it and not one who does not attend to it; by one who possesses wisdom and not by one who lacks wisdom.
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One: ‘Wisdom is to be known through discussion…’”
‘It is difficult for you, great king, being a householder dwelling in a bed crowded with children,
enjoying Kāsī sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, and accepting gold and silver—
to know whether these are arahants or those who have entered the path to arahantship.’
“By living together, great king, one’s virtue is to be known;
… [and so on] … by conversation, great king, one’s wisdom is to be known.
And that, moreover, over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted.”
“Venerable sir, these men of mine are thieves and spies who go about spying on the countryside.
What they have first gathered, I shall gather afterwards.

Now, venerable sir, having washed away that dust and dirt, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed and dressed in white garments, they will enjoy themselves, fully provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure.”
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“One should not strive in all things;
one should not become another’s man.”
One should not live dependent on another,
nor should one practice trade for a livelihood through the Dhamma. Thus ends the second [sutta].
